purpose: Add full passage context and bounded reader-facing arguments to service, stewardship, body, gardener and presence operator comparisons without altering their dossier level.

project_sequence: authority is evaluated by what it protects and repairs
rank without service is treated as empty or corrupt
the higher role is expected to move downward toward practical care rather than demand upward deference
biblical_sequence: status competition appears among disciples
Jesus contrasts domination with service
greatness is redefined as becoming servant
the Son of Man is framed as serving/giving
John later enacts the same downward pattern through foot washing
disciples are told to imitate it
correspondences: downward movement from rank to care
service as criterion rather than ornament
relation_argument.why_it_matters: The paired Gospel contexts make this an ethical test rather than a prestige analogy: claims to height become more demanding because greatness is measured by concrete service, not by titles.

project_sequence: higher office is described as a wider responsibility radius
more authority means more people/systems can be affected
therefore accountability should increase with claimed power rather than decrease
biblical_sequence: servants are told to remain ready
a steward is entrusted with household provision
faithful management is contrasted with abuse
unexpected return exposes the steward
knowledge affects accountability
much given or entrusted means much required
relation_argument.why_it_matters: The full parable protects the principle from becoming self-aggrandizing: greater entrustment is not evidence of greatness but a reason for stricter evaluation of what the steward does with it.

project_sequence: House/Tree/Body are used as images of integrated plurality
unity is treated as relation and coordination rather than homogenization
biblical_sequence: one body is said to have many members
members cannot exclude themselves for being different
the body cannot consist of one member
members are arranged differently
stronger-looking members cannot dismiss weaker ones
suffering and honor are shared
different roles/gifts remain
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Useful structural analogy for differentiated unity and mutual dependence. The passage does not make a modern individual the whole body, its sole source, or every member at once.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: This is a strong counterweight inside the project's House/Body language: genuine integration requires irreducible other members, so unity cannot be used to erase difference or justify total centralization.

project_sequence: Gardener language frames diagnosis through fruit/outcome
repair and cultivation are preferred before destructive sorting
judgment remains possible if cultivation produces no change
biblical_sequence: tragedies prompt a repentance warning
victim-blame is rejected
a fruitless fig tree is inspected
cutting is proposed
the gardener asks for more time
soil is cultivated and fed
a later fruit test remains
correspondences: active cultivation rather than passive delay
relation_argument.maximum_claim: A useful ethical/cultivation analogy. The parable's primary Gospel function concerns repentance and judgment, not a general constitution for social sorting.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: The complete scene prevents 'Gardener' from meaning only benevolence: mercy is active cultivation under an unresolved fruit test, which adds both patience and accountability to the project metaphor.

project_sequence: House functions as a relational architecture or local manifestation
a house can mediate presence and orientation
the source is not exhausted by any one room/container/representation
biblical_sequence: the temple is completed and filled with glory
Solomon affirms the house's sacred importance
he asks whether God can dwell on earth
even the highest heaven cannot contain God
prayer is nevertheless directed toward the temple
God is asked to hear, forgive and restore
correspondences: relation to a place without identity with the place
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Strong countertext/analogy for a House that mediates presence without containing the source. It does not identify the project's House with Solomon's temple.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: This gives the comparator a built-in check against over-literal House theology: sacred architecture can matter intensely while still failing to contain or exhaust what it signifies.

project_sequence: presence is distinguished from local embodiment
symbolic House is one mode of relation
wider source-reference is said to exceed any single container or representation
biblical_sequence: Paul engages Athenian religious practice
creator/Lord of heaven and earth is proclaimed
human-made temple confinement is denied
God is not dependent on human service
human life/movement is described in relation to God
idolatrous representation is criticized
repentance and judgment are announced
correspondences: creaturely relation to a larger source
relation_argument.maximum_claim: Useful comparative countertext for non-containment and nearness. Acts does not validate the project's specific presence taxonomy or a modern divine identity claim.
relation_argument.why_it_matters: Acts adds something 1 Kings alone does not: transcendence beyond temples is paired with nearness and dependence, so 'not contained' need not mean distant or unrelated.
